excerpt: This piece offers drivers essential steps for managing an auto insurance claim after a crash at one of the city's hazardous crossroads.
keyTakeaways: Columbia sits at the crossroads of I-20, I-26, and I-77, and its interchange complexes — particularly the I-20/I-26 junction known as "Malfunction Junction" — handle traffic volumes that exceed their design capacity. South Carolina's three-year statute of limitations (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) and modified comparative fault rule (less than 51% at fault) govern how victims recover compensation for injuries caused at these high-risk crossroads.

faqs.question: What is the most dangerous intersection in Columbia, SC?
faqs.answer: The I-20 and US-76 (Broad River Road) interchange and the I-20/I-26 junction known as “Malfunction Junction” are the two locations most consistently identified as Columbia's worst. Both handle traffic volumes that exceed their design capacity, and both require drivers to merge and weave across multiple lanes at highway speed. We do not attach single-year collision counts to them here, because the figures in circulation cannot be tied to a stated reporting period or source.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a car accident lawsuit in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: Under S.C. Code § 15-3-530, you have three years from the date of your accident to file a personal injury lawsuit in South Carolina. Missing the statute of limitations typically means losing your right to compensation entirely.

faqs.question: Can I still recover compensation if I was partially at fault for a Columbia intersection crash?
faqs.answer: Yes. South Carolina follows a modified comparative fault rule that allows you to recover compensation as long as you are less than 51% at fault for the accident. Your total award is reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you are 25% at fault and your damages total $200,000, you would recover $150,000.

faqs.question: Why is the I-20/I-26 interchange called Malfunction Junction?
faqs.answer: The I-20/I-26 interchange earned the nickname "Malfunction Junction" because of its history of frequent, serious collisions caused by its tight curves, short merge zones, high traffic volumes, and confusing lane configurations. The interchange sits at the center of South Carolina's interstate system and handles a mix of commuter and heavy commercial truck traffic that regularly exceeds its design capacity.

faqs.question: What should I do immediately after a car accident in Columbia?
faqs.answer: Call 911, seek medical treatment even if you feel fine, photograph the scene and all vehicle damage, collect witness contact information, do not admit fault, and contact a Columbia car accident lawyer before giving any recorded statements to insurance companies. South Carolina law requires you to notify police immediately after a crash that injures or kills anyone (S.C. Code § 56-5-1260). If no officer investigated a crash involving injury or $1,000 or more in property damage, the driver or owner must file a written report with the DMV within 15 days (S.C. Code § 56-5-1270).

faqs.question: Can I sue if dangerous road design caused my Columbia accident?
faqs.answer: Potentially, yes. If a government entity's failure to properly design, maintain, or signal an intersection contributed to your crash, you may have a claim against the City of Columbia, Richland County, or the South Carolina Department of Transportation. These governmental tort claims must be filed within two years under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act, so consulting an attorney promptly is critical.
